correctness.rationale: The common phase and modulation normalize the first two coefficients uniquely. Independently, for (1,1,u,v) the positive-frequency autocorrelations are r₁=1+u+v/u, r₂=u+v, and r₃=v; r₀=4. The zero coefficient of |P|⁶ is 4³+24Σ|r_j|²+6 Re(r₁² conjugate(r₂))+12 Re(r₁r₂ conjugate(r₃)), with the sum over j=1,2,3. For x=(ψ−φ)/2, y=(ψ−3φ)/2 and c=cos x, one has r₁=e^(ix)(2c+e^(−iy)), r₂=2c e^(i(2x−y)), r₃=e^(i(3x−y)); substitution gives 112+288c²+(132c+48c³)cos y. The real change of variables is invertible, so choosing the minimizing cos y is attainable at every |c|. The remaining cubic is strictly convex on [0,1], has negative derivative at 0 and positive derivative at 1, and its unique stationary point there is (12−√111)/6. Substitution gives 616−(148/3)√111; the stated decimal agrees. At this nonzero point, equality forces y in πZ, v=u³, and cos φ=−|c|, yielding precisely two normalized conjugate orbits. Conversely these phases attain the bound. The same correlations give the fourth power 20+16c²+8c cos y, uniquely minimized in |c| at 1/4 with minimum 19, verifying the optimizer distinction without relying on samples.
residual_risks: Only continuous probability Haar measure and the four consecutive frequencies are proved; no formal certificate or finite-alphabet optimum is claimed in the original.

value.rationale: As mathematics, sharp moment optimization on consecutive frequencies at fixed coefficient moduli is a motivated flatness problem. The full phase rigidity and the different fourth and sixth optimal phases teach more than the small numerical improvement alone: fourth-moment optimization does not exactly solve the sixth-moment objective even at this aperture. This is intrinsic value of the result, not evidence of additional value from another report of the same theorem.
